A learning archive

Elder Pauline Shirt and the school she began in her living room

Nimkiiquay, Thunder Woman · Plains Cree, Red-Tail Hawk Clan · 1943–2024

Pauline Shirt came to Toronto from Saddle Lake, Alberta, in the late 1960s. In 1976 she and Vern Harper opened Wandering Spirit Survival School so that Indigenous children in the city could learn in their own ways. That school is now Kâpapâmahchakwêw – Wandering Spirit School. This archive gathers her life, her work in community, and the school's history in one place.

Folder 1

Her life and her work in community

Teacher, organizer, founder, healer, singer, Grandmother. Pauline Shirt worked in Toronto's Indigenous community for more than fifty years.

1943 – 1960s
Saddle Lake

A farm, a language, a father who spoke Cree to the horses

Pauline Shirt was born on July 13, 1943, at Saddle Lake Cree Nation in Alberta. Her parents were Louisa and Felix. She was Plains Cree, of the Red-Tail Hawk Clan.

She grew up on a farm, working beside her father. He spoke Cree to the animals, the horses and the plants, and he taught her about the land. The family worked together, and she carried that way of working into everything she built later.

At eight she was sent to Blue Quills, a Catholic-run residential school at St. Paul, Alberta. Her mother worked there as an assistant cook, so Pauline had a parent close by, which most children did not. She was pressed to become a good Catholic girl. She kept speaking Cree. The Toronto District School Board describes her as a residential school survivor.

She finished high school in Edmonton and went on to business college.

Late 1960s
Toronto

Arriving in the city

Pauline came to Toronto in the late 1960s with three young children. She found her way to the Native Canadian Centre of Toronto and to a circle of educators and leaders that included Jim Dumont, Edna Manitowabi and Joe Hare. She began teaching and lecturing in those years and did not stop.

1974
Vancouver to Ottawa

The Native People's Caravan

In 1974 Pauline and Vern Harper organized the Ontario leg of the Native People's Caravan, which crossed the country from Vancouver to Ottawa in support of Indigenous land and water rights. The Caravan carried a manifesto that called for Indigenous control of Indigenous education.

Vern Harper's book about the journey, Following the Red Path, shows her at work throughout. She took the phone call in Toronto from Indian Rights for Indian Women offering food and money. She helped organize the meal that met the travellers at Harbord Collegiate. She brought the children to Ottawa and stood at the front on Parliament Hill on September 30. Afterwards, at the Native People's Embassy, she and Vern helped care for about thirty children in the nursery.

“one of the strongest believers and workers in the Caravan”Vern Harper on Pauline, in the author's note to Following the Red Path (1979)

The day after the demonstration on the Hill was met with force, on October 1, 1974, Pauline decided at the Embassy that she would start her own school in Toronto.

1976
A living room

Founding a school

Her son Clayton had refused to go back to public school. The bullying in the schoolyard was racist, and the curriculum ignored Indigenous cultures. Pauline began teaching children in her own living room and paid for it from her savings. By September 1976 the school had a classroom at the Native Canadian Centre and a name: Wandering Spirit Survival School.

When the Toronto Board of Education voted on whether to accept the school in 1977, the debate was tense. Pauline stepped out of the room, offered tobacco and prayed to her grandfather. She also promised the Board she would take no salary for seven years.

The school's full story is in Folder 2.

1984
Healing

Red Willow

In 1984 Pauline founded Red Willow, described as the first independent clinic of Indigenous holistic practitioners. She had been part of an Indigenous Medicine Society since the early 1980s and was a member of the Three Fires Society (Midewiwin) and the Buffalo Dance Society. George Brown College notes that she held a degree in sacred Indigenous Knowledge, which it compares to a doctorate.

1980s – 2024
Grandmother

Grandma Pauline

For decades Pauline mentored young people and young families in Toronto as a Grandmother. She opened gatherings with prayer and sat in meetings with every level of government. She spoke and sang in Cree. She lived for many years at the Bain Co-op in Riverdale and raised five children.

George Brown College

Guiding Elder and Knowledge and Wisdom Keeper. She took Indigenous students under her wing, made work plans with them that centred on spiritual well-being, and helped shape the college's Indigenous Education Strategy. Students, staff and alumni called her Grandma Pauline.

Urban Indigenous Education Centre

Member of the Elders Council that guides Indigenous education across the Toronto District School Board. The council was formed in 2014.

imagineNATIVE

Cultural advisor to the imagineNATIVE Film + Media Arts Festival, which remembered her as a beacon of inspiration.

Her own school

She withdrew from the school around 1989 because of illness. She lived to see it reclaim its first name in 2019 and teach its first Grade 12 class.

“Show it with the work.”A saying of Pauline's, recalled by George Brown College

2021 – 2023
Honours

Recognition

  • Order of Ontario. Named among the 26 appointees for 2022 and invested by Lieutenant Governor Edith Dumont on November 27, 2023, for a lifetime of work in Indigenous education, cultural revitalization and holistic wellness.
  • A portrait by Kent Monkman. The Cree artist painted her for his exhibition Being Legendary at the Royal Ontario Museum, October 2022 to April 2023.
  • A mural at the Bickford Centre. Painted by Johl Whiteduck Ringuette and Lara Lucretia, near Christie Pits.
  • A chapter in Indigenous Toronto. Kerry Potts sat with Pauline to record her vision for the school (Coach House Books, 2021).
2024 onward
Carried forward

What continues

Pauline Shirt passed into the Spirit World on May 7, 2024, at the age of 80. A sacred fire was lit for Grandmother Pauline at Kâpapâmahchakwêw – Wandering Spirit School.

Her daughter Luana has said her mother's legacy lives on in the family. It also lives in a school that now graduates its own Grade 12 students, and in Nimkii-Kwe Akiing, Thunder Women on the Land, a two-week summer cultural camp for First Nations, Métis and Inuit secondary students held in her name at Albion Hills and led by Elder Clayton Shirt with the Urban Indigenous Education Centre.

Folder 2

The school: from a living room to JK–12

Kâpapâmahchakwêw – Wandering Spirit School is often described as the first Indigenous-led school in Canada. Its records show a community that kept asking a school board for the right to teach its own children its own way, and kept winning ground.

Why

Parents saw their children being taught out of themselves

An early profile of the school, kept in the Board's historical file, records the reasons in the parents' own terms. Their children complained of discrimination. Teachers had no training to deal with it. Nothing in the regular program taught the heritage of Indigenous peoples, and parents felt the system was assimilating their children.

For Pauline it was personal. Her son Clayton refused to go back. She and Vern Harper looked for a school that would be culturally safe for him and found none, so they made one.

The model was the Red School House in St. Paul, Minnesota, a survival school founded through the American Indian Movement by Eddie Benton-Banai. A council of seven parents advised her, and Nora Keeshig-Tobias, Keith Lickers, Al Bigwin and Jim Dumont helped develop the curriculum.

1976 – 1977

Opening, and asking the Board in

The school opened in September 1976 as a self-supporting private school at the Native Canadian Centre of Toronto. When the Board of Education first wrote it down, it had ten pupils aged five to fourteen, one qualified teacher, a supply teacher and several volunteers, and its own board of five trustees.

On January 27, 1977, the Board's Alternatives in Education Committee recommended accepting Wandering Spirit Survival School as an alternative school. The conditions were a qualified teacher acceptable to both the school's trustees and the Board, suitable space, and open enrolment by September 1978. The founders had asked that only Native children be enrolled at first, with the school later open to any child while keeping its cultural identity.

The Board accepted the school early in 1977 and found it a classroom on the third floor of Winchester Public School.

How it taught

Native Way education

The school's 1981 brochure calls it a Native Way School, where Native and non-Native children learned basic academic skills with the heritage, spiritual and cultural sides of Native life at the centre.

  • The whole year's curriculum was built around the Four Seasons. Pauline described a Four Seasons Curriculum of language, ceremony, community and love.
  • Mornings were for culture and Native language. Afternoons were for the basic skills.
  • By 1981 it taught in three languages, Ojibwe, English and French, and had added Kindergarten.
  • Standards of behaviour followed the teaching of spiritual leaders in the Native community.
  • Parents had to take part. It was a condition of enrolment. A council of parents, supporters and a student representative governed school policy.

“You have to know your creation story.”Pauline Shirt, speaking with Kerry Potts about where curriculum, songs and spirit come from

1982 – 1985

Winning self-determination, one motion at a time

The Board's minutes from these years read as a long negotiation over who decides. In November 1982 trustees approved in principle a new category of school, the Native People's Survival School, distinct from every other school in Toronto and meant to give the school's council as much local autonomy as the Education Act allowed.

In 1983 the Board recognized Wandering Spirit as a Cultural Survival/Native Way program and no longer simply an alternative school.

On May 30, 1985, the school's Executive Council asked the Board to recognize the need for Native Way Teachers, to hire three by that September, and to treat Wandering Spirit as a school serving the whole city. Trustees approved the proposal in principle by a recorded vote of 18 to 0. The policy that followed helped carry Native Way education into other schools.

Three names

1976 – 1989

Wandering Spirit Survival School

Named by Pauline for the Cree war chief Kâpapâmahchakwêw.

1989 – 2019

First Nations School of Toronto

The change took effect July 1, 1989. The new name was unveiled at 155 College Street on September 28.

2019 – today

Kâpapâmahchakwêw – Wandering Spirit School

Reclaimed in a ceremony in February 2019, this time in Cree first.

Where the school has lived

  1. 1976
    Pauline's living roomPaid for from her savings.
  2. Sept. 1976
    Native Canadian Centre of TorontoA room on Spadina Road, until the Centre needed the space back.
  3. 1977
    Winchester Public School, 15 Prospect StreetOne large third-floor classroom, split into a junior and a senior side.
  4. 1978
    Sackville Public School, 19 Sackville StreetThe second floor, approved in October 1978 once enrolment could reach 25. Shared with Inglenook Community School.
  5. 1989 – 2017
    Not yet documented hereThe school moved more than once in these years. The sources gathered so far do not name the addresses.
  6. 2017 – today
    16 Phin AvenueThe former Eastern Commerce Collegiate, shared with the Urban Indigenous Education Centre. Grade 9 began in 2017 and Grade 12 in 2021–22.
  7. Next
    A home built for itSince 2017 the Board has sought a new building. In 2021 it chose a standalone, fully Indigenized JK–12 school over a retrofit, and in 2025 its Chair and Elder Dr. Duke Redbird asked both governments to fund it.
The founders

Pauline Shirt, Nimkiiquay (1943–2024)

Plains Cree from Saddle Lake, Alberta. Founder and volunteer teacher of Native history, language and tradition.

Vern Harper, Asin (1936–2018)

Cree Elder born in Toronto, known as the Urban Elder. President of the school's council, author of Following the Red Path, and later an Elder with the Board's Aboriginal Education Centre.

Portraits as reproduced in the 2023 Inglenook commemoration proposal.

2008 – today

The wider work: from one school to a whole board

The question the school raised in 1976 did not stay inside one building. In 2008 the Toronto District School Board formed its Aboriginal Education Centre and joined the provincial Urban Aboriginal Education Pilot Project. The Centre's Elders Council followed in 2014. In 2018 the Centre became the Urban Indigenous Education Centre, which now shares 16 Phin Avenue with the school.

Decolonizing Our Schools, the 2010 report on that pilot by Dr. Susan D. Dion with Krista Johnston and Dr. Carla Rice, drew on more than 200 students, parents, teachers and community members. It found that schools were still failing Indigenous students, and that the answer lay in student well-being, teacher learning, changed school environments and making Indigenous education a priority across the Board. Parents at Wandering Spirit had said much the same thirty-four years earlier.

    Folder 6

    The name: Kâpapâmahchakwêw

    The school carries the name of a Plains Cree war chief. Pauline chose it on purpose, and the reason reaches back to her own home community.

    c. 1845 – 1885

    Wandering Spirit

    Kâpapâmahchakwêw, Wandering Spirit, was war chief in the band that followed Mistahimaskwa, Big Bear. War chief was a separate office from Big Bear's, earned in battle, and it made him head of the warrior society.

    By 1885 the buffalo were gone and government rations were being withheld from hungry people. On April 2 of that year, at Frog Lake, warriors led by Wandering Spirit and Big Bear's son confronted the Indian agent who had refused them food. The agent and other settlers were killed. The band then took Fort Pitt and fought Canadian troops near Frenchman Butte. Wandering Spirit later surrendered and was hanged at Battleford on November 27, 1885.

    The accounts do not agree on everything. Some tie him to Louis Riel's resistance and others say he and Big Bear turned Riel down. One account, in Sharon Berg's book about the school, holds that he took the blame for a shooting to protect a younger man.

    Six generations

    A name that went unspoken

    At Saddle Lake his name was not said aloud for close to six generations. Pauline's family carried shame from the charge that he had killed one of his own.

    Pauline named her school after him so that his name would be spoken again, with honour, by children. To her he stood for a spirit she wanted her own children and community to have. The school's 1981 brochure says he was known for “protecting his people's way of life.”

    When she chose the name she did not yet know how closely she was related to him. She learned later that he was her own grandfather, several generations back.

    2019

    Spoken again

    For thirty years the school was called First Nations School of Toronto. In February 2019 it held a ceremony and took back its first name, now in Cree as well as English: Kâpapâmahchakwêw – Wandering Spirit School.

    Questions for talking about the name with students are in Folder 7.

    Folder 7

    For learning

    Reflection prompts written for this archive. They are starting points. Choose who is in the room.

      Names and terms

      Nimkiiquay
      Pauline Shirt's name, Thunder Woman. Also written Nimikiiquay.
      Kâpapâmahchakwêw
      Wandering Spirit, the Cree war chief the school is named for. Older records spell it without accents.
      Asin
      Vern Harper's Cree name, also written Asini.
      Mistahimaskwa
      Big Bear, the Plains Cree chief whose band Wandering Spirit belonged to.
      Survival school
      A school founded by Indigenous parents in the 1970s so that language, culture and identity would survive. The Red School House in Minnesota was the model for Wandering Spirit.
      Native Way education
      The school's own term for teaching through the seasons, language, ceremony and community alongside academic skills.
      Native Way Teacher
      A teaching position the school's council asked the Board to recognize and staff in 1985.
      Nimkii-Kwe Akiing
      Thunder Women on the Land, the summer cultural camp held in Pauline's name.
      UIEC
      The Urban Indigenous Education Centre of the Toronto District School Board, guided by its Elders Council.
      KWSS
      Kâpapâmahchakwêw – Wandering Spirit School.
      Folder 8

      Sources and notes on the record

      Links open the original outside the archive.

        Where the records differ

        An archive should show its seams. Families, Elders and staff who know more are invited to correct these.

        1976 or 1977?

        The school opened in September 1976. The Board accepted it in early 1977, which is why some Board pages give 1977 as the founding year.

        January or February?

        The committee recommended approval on January 27, 1977. Later minutes say January and the school's brochure says February. The printed minutes page is headed February 10, 1976, a misprint for 1977.

        Ten students or fourteen?

        The 1977 minutes count ten pupils. A profile written about a year later says fourteen.

        One centre, three names

        Board records call the first classroom's host the Native Friendship Centre and the Centre for Native Peoples. The school's own brochure says the Native Canadian Centre of Toronto.

        Order of Ontario: 2022 or 2023?

        Both. Pauline was one of the Order's 2022 appointees. The list was announced on November 6, 2023, and she was invested that November 27.

        1989 to 2017

        The sources gathered here do not name where the school was housed between Sackville Street and Phin Avenue. This is the largest gap in the archive.

        Photographs

        The portraits of Pauline Shirt and Vern Harper and the 1983 photograph come from the 2023 Inglenook proposal, which does not credit photographers. Please confirm permission with the families before wider publication.

        Wandering Spirit's story

        Written accounts of 1885 come mostly from settler and court records and they conflict. The account closest to Pauline's own is in Kerry Potts's chapter and Sharon Berg's book The Name Unspoken (2019).
